lines.text: This is Atlas. The personal AI computer.
It sits on your desk, learns how you live, and works for you. It remembers what matters, answers in plain words, and adapts as your life changes.
Everything it knows about you stays on the device in front of you.
Inside, a camera on top, a speaker in front, and a Jetson that runs the vision, the memory, and an agent that acts on your behalf, like a squire.
Point it at your week. Atlas reads your classes and your calendar, and sees how the day really goes at the desk.
Each morning it briefs you. What is first, when to leave, the walk drawn on the map. Fall behind, and it re-plans. One tap puts the new plan on your calendar.
It notices your breaks, asks whether it guessed right, and learns what pulls you away.
Ask where you left your keys. It answers in seconds, with the frame it saw them in.
It can just talk, do your arithmetic, or look something up and cite its sources.
You would expect the model on the box to be small. It is not. A highly capable Qwen runs right here. Fast, accurate, and private. Forty-two demo questions, forty-two right.
And when your life needs something new, Atlas learns the tool. You describe the task, and the lab teaches it from your own examples.
The lab is two AMD Strix Halo pods. One is your trainer. It fine-tunes your own model on your own examples.
The other is the network's trainer. With everyone's consent, it learns from everyone's examples, so every Atlas gets better together.
A test decides whether the new model is really better. Only then does it ship back. Our adapter is public on Hugging Face.
Everything live runs on the Jetson. A face is blurred the moment a picture would leave the device, so what travels is never a face.
Pull the network cable. It keeps seeing, remembering, alerting and answering. Only learning pauses.
And it keeps a ledger of what left. Tonight, thirteen destinations allowed, thirteen blocked.
Point it at the kitchen. The bin camera sees a can go in the trash, and Atlas knows the rule. At UCF, cans go in recycling.
It keeps the count. Four of six recyclables made it this week, sixty-seven percent against a goal of eighty. A nudge, a game called Sort It, and the number moves.
Only counts leave the box. Never pictures.
Point it at your friends. Each Atlas keeps its owner's calendar private.
Ask for a time for everyone, and the boxes talk. Free. Busy then, how about three. Agreed, three of three in. Only free or busy leaves each box.
Same box, other lives. A night-shift worker. A family home. A plant operator whose robot inspections it reads offline, cited to the row.
And Day Run. Play tomorrow before you live it, on a map of your own campus.
Atlas. The personal AI computer. It learns you, and keeps you to itself.
